Clermont-Ferrand|France.f: Michelin factories once employed up to 30,000 workers here, and much of the city is built from black volcanic Volvic stone.

Figari|France.f: Vines have grown here since the Roman era, and 153 hectares now produce Vin de Corse-Figari AOC wine.

Grenoble|France.f: Renamed Gratianopolis after Emperor Gratian's visit in 381 AD, the name wore down over the centuries into Grenoble.

Deauville|France.f: The Promenade des Planches, the wooden boardwalk along the beach, was completed in 1923.

Limoges|France.f: Kaolin found near Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche in 1765 launched Limoges porcelain, long after its enamels began exporting in the 12th century.

Pau|France.f: Pau is the only city in Europe where two founders of royal dynasties were born, Henry IV of France and Sweden's Charles XIV John.

Metz|France.f: Metz Cathedral has the largest expanse of stained glass in the world, about 6,500 square metres, including windows by Chagall.

Perpignan|France.f: Salvador Dali declared Perpignan's railway station the Cosmic Centre of the Universe after a vision there in 1963.

Nîmes|France.f: Denim takes its name from this city, from the French serge de Nimes.

Tours|France.f: Tours was the temporary seat of the French government from 10 to 13 June 1940, before it moved on to Bordeaux.

Poitiers|France.f: The 4th century Baptistery of Saint-Jean in Poitiers is described as the oldest church in France.

Calvi|France.f: Local legend says Christopher Columbus came from Calvi, then Genoese, and the Foreign Legion's 2nd Parachute Regiment is based nearby.

La Rochelle|France.f: Cardinal Richelieu blockaded La Rochelle for 14 months in 1627 and 1628, until it surrendered and lost its mayor and privileges.

Dole|France.f: Louis Pasteur was born in Dole, which was capital of Franche-Comte until Louis XIV moved the parlement to Besancon.

Bergerac|France.f: Bergerac has two statues of Cyrano de Bergerac, and its region holds twelve wine AOCs including Monbazillac and Pecharmant.

Toulon|France.f: French naval officers scuttled the fleet based at Toulon on 27 November 1942 to keep it out of German hands.

Rennes|France.f: From 2002 to 2008 Rennes was the smallest city in the world with a metro, a driverless line 9.4 km long.

Brive|France.f: Brive-la-Gaillarde was a regional capital of the French Resistance, seat of several clandestine information networks.

Carcassonne|France.f: The Cite of Carcassonne has a double ring of walls with 52 towers, restored by Viollet-le-Duc between 1853 and 1879.

Rodez|France.f: Starting in 1792, Delambre measured the arc from Dunkirk to Rodez in the survey that helped define the metre.

Chambéry|France.f: Chambery was the capital of the House of Savoy's lands from 1295 to 1563, and its Elephants Fountain dates from 1838.

Caen|France.f: William the Conqueror is buried in Caen, which took 14 years, from 1948 to 1962, to rebuild after the 1944 bombing.

Avignon|France.f: Seven successive popes lived in Avignon between 1309 and 1377, and Clement VI bought the city from Joanna I of Naples in 1348.

Castres|France.f: Castres holds the Goya Museum, created in 1840, with the largest collection of Spanish paintings in France.

Béziers|France.f: The Canal du Midi crosses the river Orb at Beziers on an aqueduct claimed to be the first of its kind.

Aurillac|France.f: Aurillac was once the French capital of umbrellas, making half of French production, some 250,000 units in 1999.

Annecy|France.f: Annecy is sometimes called the Venice of the Alps for the three canals and the Thiou river running through its old city.

Le Puy-en-Velay|France.f: Le Puy-en-Velay is a starting point for the pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela, a walk of some 1600 km.

Saint-Tropez|France.f: Saint-Tropez takes its name from the early Christian martyr Saint Torpes, whose body reportedly arrived by boat in Nero's reign.

Ushant|France.f: Ushant is the westernmost point of metropolitan France, and its Ouessant sheep are one of the smallest breeds of domestic sheep.
